# Artifact Keeper 1.8.1

A patch release with **one data-loss fix you should read before upgrading**, security updates to the bundled scanner binaries, one security fix, and a reporting fix. No schema migrations.

## Read this first — Maven storage GC could delete hand-repaired objects

If you have ever repaired a Maven 404 by inserting a row into `maven_flat_object_owner`, **that object may already be gone**, and you should read this whole section.

Since 1.7.0 the orphan Maven flat-object sweep enumerated its delete candidates from `maven_flat_object_owner` and tested only catalog anchors. But since #2574/#2585 an owner row is also what makes a legacy row-less object *readable* — and inserting one is the documented remediation for keys the catalog-only backfill cannot see. For exactly that class every arm of the predicate was true by construction and permanently, so **the row that made an object servable was the row that queued it for deletion**. An operator who fixed a fail-closed 404 by attributing the key got a 200 for one hour, then lost the bytes.

**Two changes close it:**

1. The sweep now reclaims only rows the system wrote and can re-derive — `primary_row`, `metadata_files`, `derived_checksum`, `metadata_rollup`, `write_claim`. Those are caches over other catalog state and are stale by definition once their anchors vanish. An operator-inserted row is a primary record, and **any source value the system does not write is now protected**, including ones a future external tool might stamp.
2. The sweep is **opt-in**, behind `MAVEN_FLAT_GC_ENABLED`. Unset, it reports what it would reclaim and deletes nothing — matching the OCI blob sweep's existing posture of biasing toward leaking storage over losing data. On a migrated instance, catalog absence is the *expected* state of legitimate legacy data; that is why the attribution table exists, so absence alone must not be treated as proof of garbage.

**Affected versions:** 1.7.0 through 1.8.0. Severity was not uniform — before 1.7.3 the candidate scan frequently never completed on large attribution tables, largely masking it. The 1.7.3 guard rebuild made the scan complete, so **an operator who upgraded to 1.7.3+ for those guard fixes received mass reclamation of hand-repaired data as a side effect.**

**If you may be affected:** there is no recovery from within Artifact Keeper — the sweep hard-deletes the object and its attribution row together, with no tombstone or journal. Recovery depends on storage-side retention: S3/GCS/Azure object versioning, a lifecycle noncurrent window, a bucket replica, or a filesystem backup. Each reclaim did emit `Storage GC: reclaimed orphaned row-less Maven flat object` at INFO with the `storage_key`, so a backend log with sufficient retention reconstructs the key list to restore from.

The same fix ships on the 1.7 line as **1.7.8**. (It was originally tagged as 1.7.7, but that tag published nothing — its Docker Publish failed on the scanner CVEs described in the next section, and release tags are immutable, so 1.7.8 supersedes it. See #3466.)

## Security — bundled scanner binaries

The vulnerability scanners shipped inside our images carried known-vulnerable Go dependencies. These are **CVEs in bundled third-party tooling, not in Artifact Keeper's own code**, and none is reachable through the Artifact Keeper API. They are called out here because clearing them is what let 1.8.1 be published at all: the Docker Publish Security Scan gate failed on them for two consecutive runs, every manifest-merge job was skipped as a result, and **no images published from `main` between 2026-08-19 and these fixes**.

- **`usr/local/bin/trivy`** in the scanner-adapter image: **10 HIGH cleared**. Six are Go stdlib against the go1.26.5 build (`CVE-2026-33818`, `-56853`, `-56858`, `-56859`, `-56860`, `-56862`), two are `golang.org/x/net` (`CVE-2026-39821` in `x/net/idna`, and `CVE-2026-46600`), and two are `golang.org/x/mod` (`CVE-2026-56864`, `CVE-2026-56865`). Only the first six are standard library; the other four are modules, which is why a toolchain bump alone would not have reached them. The adapter now bundles a rebuild of upstream Trivy v0.74.0 on go1.26.7, which pins `x/mod` v0.40.0 itself, and all ten clear at the source. Measured against an identical vulnerability DB the binary goes 10 HIGH → 0 at the gate's settings, and 11 → 1 at all severities with no ignore file; the survivor is `GO-2026-5932` in `x/crypto`, which has no fixed version and is UNKNOWN severity. The rebuilt scanner-adapter image is published as **1.2.7**.

  All ten were live at this line's gate — none of them is suppressed in `main`'s `.trivyignore`. This differs from the 1.7 line, where `CVE-2026-39821` and `CVE-2026-46600` are still live suppressions and the gate therefore only ever saw eight of the ten. On `main` both were retired to tombstones when the grype build moved to a floored Go toolchain, so nothing was hiding them here.

- **`usr/local/bin/scanner-adapter`**, the adapter's own binary: **already clean on this line, and still clean.** The adapter's Go stage builds on the floating `golang:1.26-alpine` tag, which currently resolves to go1.26.6, so it carried none of the six stdlib HIGHs. That build stage now asserts a minimum Go toolchain patch anyway, matching the backend images. **This floor fixes nothing that was live on 1.8.x — it is a regression guard**, so a lagging mirror or a stale builder cache fails the build loudly instead of shipping a vulnerable stdlib silently. It is not hypothetical: the 1.7 line's adapter binary (1.2.3) was published before go1.26.6 existed and carried the same six stdlib HIGHs, which is exactly the failure a floating tag with no floor permits.

- **`usr/local/bin/grype`** in the backend image: the same `x/mod` pair (`CVE-2026-56864`, `CVE-2026-56865`) cleared, by overriding the module to v0.40.0 in the build. No upstream Grype release carries this bump — v0.117.0 is the newest release and even Grype's `main` still pins v0.38.0 — so an explicit override was the only source-level fix available. `grype --version` still reports 0.117.0 and the DB schema is unchanged, so the recorded `scanner_version` and the build-time seeded DB are unaffected.

**On severity, honestly:** both `x/mod` advisories are scoped to `x/mod/sumdb` and `sumdb/tlog` — the checksum-database transparency-log client — and neither package is linked into the Grype binary at all; `go mod why` reports that the main module does not need it. Trivy reports Go binaries at module granularity from the embedded build info, so it flags the dependency version regardless of whether the vulnerable code is reachable, and `govulncheck` would call the binary unaffected. We fixed at the source rather than suppressing, but **no Artifact Keeper deployment was exploitable through this.**

## Security

**RUSTSEC-2026-0258** — the bundled `h2` HTTP/2 implementation is updated from 0.4.13 to 0.4.16, closing an unbounded-empty-DATA-frame denial of service. This is worth taking promptly on any instance whose gRPC port is reachable from an untrusted network: `tonic` serves h2c only, with no TLS or upgrade negotiation, so the frame decoder is reached **before any application authentication runs**. Every prior release is affected. Upstream rates it Low — the frames are empty, so an attacker trades bandwidth for the server's per-frame bookkeeping rather than for payload.

## Fixed

**Proxied downloads are counted again.** The Downloads column read 0 for proxy and remote repositories in most formats, because the serve paths never recorded a download. Docker/OCI, cargo, NuGet, Debian, Helm and Go now record proxied serves, joining PyPI, npm, Maven, Ansible, Conda, CRAN, RPM and RubyGems. A class-level guard now fails the build if a new proxy serve path records nothing without an explicit marker, so the remaining formats are tracked rather than forgotten — see #3446 for the current list.
